The International Space Station is the largest structure humanity has ever built in space and the place every thread of the space age converges. Its Russian core descends directly from Salyut and Mir; its American segment from Skylab; it was assembled by the Space Shuttle, is crewed by Soyuz, resupplied by the descendants of the Progress freighter, and carries laboratories built by Europe and Japan — nearly every earlier program present in it as heritage. Assembled from 1998 and continuously crewed since November 2000, it is the longest unbroken human presence off Earth in history, and the clearest proof of a single idea: that the greatest things in space are built not by winning a race but by former rivals choosing, decade after decade, to build them together.

The International Space Station — humanity’s longest continuously crewed habitat, occupied since November 2000. Assembled across more than 40 launches by NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. Currently scheduled for deorbit around 2031.
First Chinese space station; single-module testbed
Last Almaz military station — Soyuz 21 + Soyuz 24 crews; Soyuz 23 failed approach; reentered 1977-08-08 after 412 days

Humanity's permanent home in orbit. 420 tonnes, 109-metre wingspan. Built by 16 nations across 42 flights. Has hosted 290 people from 26 countries. Visible to the naked eye from Earth — the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus.
